lesson.title: A Different Recipe: Vertex Form and Why It's Useful
lesson.summary: Vertex form, a(x-h)^2 + k, writes a quadratic so its vertex, (h, k), is visible directly in the equation, and completing the square lets you convert any quadratic from standard form into this shape.
lesson.body:
Standard form is convenient for reading the y-intercept at a glance, but finding the vertex still takes a calculation, x = -b/(2a), then substituting back. Vertex form skips that step entirely by building the vertex right into the equation: f(x) = a(x - h)^2 + k, where the vertex is simply the point (h, k). The role of a is the same as in standard form, its sign tells you whether the parabola opens upward or downward, and its size tells you how narrow or wide the curve is.

To convert a quadratic from standard form into vertex form, you complete the square. Take the running example from earlier in this chapter, f(x) = x^2 - 4x + 3. Group the x^2 and x terms together: (x^2 - 4x) + 3. Take half of the coefficient on x, which is -4, giving -2, then square that result: (-2)^2 = 4. Add and subtract that 4 inside the expression so you have not changed its value: (x^2 - 4x + 4 - 4) + 3. The first three terms now form a perfect square: (x - 2)^2 - 4 + 3, which simplifies to (x - 2)^2 - 1.

So f(x) = x^2 - 4x + 3 in vertex form is f(x) = (x - 2)^2 - 1, meaning h = 2 and k = -1, so the vertex is (2, -1). Compare that to the vertex section earlier in this chapter, where you found the exact same vertex, (2, -1), by computing x = -b/(2a) = 4/2 = 2 and then f(2) = -1 directly from standard form. Two completely different methods, one from standard form using the formula, one from completing the square into vertex form, land on the identical point, which is exactly the kind of agreement that confirms both methods are correct.

You can also always check a conversion by expanding vertex form back out. (x - 2)^2 - 1 = (x - 2)(x - 2) - 1 = x^2 - 4x + 4 - 1 = x^2 - 4x + 3, which matches the original standard form exactly. As a second example with a coefficient other than 1, take vertex form 2(x - 3)^2 + 4. Expanding: 2(x^2 - 6x + 9) + 4 = 2x^2 - 12x + 18 + 4 = 2x^2 - 12x + 22, standard form with a = 2, b = -12, c = 22. Check the vertex formula against this: x = -b/(2a) = 12/4 = 3, and f(3) = 2(9) - 12(3) + 22 = 18 - 36 + 22 = 4, giving vertex (3, 4), exactly the (h, k) = (3, 4) that vertex form already told you. Whichever direction you convert, both forms describe the exact same parabola, they just make different information easy to read.
